reviewNote: Guidance here changes. Re-verify against DanceSafe, LAPPA, and manufacturer instructions before each release. Conflicts between sources are recorded rather than resolved.

framing.headline: Testing finds red flags. It never gives a green light.
canBullets: Tell you something you did not expect is present
Tell you the substance may not be what it was sold as
Give you information to decide how much to take, or whether to take it
cannotBullets: Tell you how strong it is
Tell you how pure it is
Tell you everything that is in it
Tell you whether fentanyl is in it
Read a bag the way a lab reads a reference sample
framing.ruleInRuleOut: A test can rule a substance IN. It cannot rule every other substance OUT.

sources.name: DanceSafe — Drug checking
Crew — Drug testing and checking

prevalence.headline: How often fentanyl actually turns up

rows.what: Sold as heroin or another opioid

rows.note: The bigger danger is that the amount varies wildly from pill to pill in the same batch.
Not zero, and worth testing — but not most.
One study of 53 samples found none.
Repeated investigations of alarming reports have not produced a single laboratory-confirmed case.

prevalence.coUse: You will also see that fentanyl appears alongside cocaine or meth in a huge share of overdose deaths. That is true, but it mostly reflects people using both — deliberately or at different times — not stimulants being secretly cut. The supply figures above and the death figures cannot both be explained by contamination. In one San Francisco study of overdoses, about 43% of people had not intended to take an opioid; the majority had.
prevalence.regional: These are national averages and they move. What is in the supply where you are can look nothing like the country as a whole, and it changes within months. Local drug-checking data beats any national number.
prevalence.bottomLine: The reason to test is not that everything is contaminated — it is that you cannot tell by looking. Testing is the only way to know what you are actually holding, and knowing changes what you can do about it.

sources.name: Russell et al. — fentanyl in stimulant samples, 25 states
Nguyen et al. — intent in non-fatal overdose, J Urban Health
UNC Street Drug Analysis Lab — The Year in Drugs
National Harm Reduction Coalition — fentanyl

strips.name: Fentanyl test strips
strips.detects: Fentanyl and many — not all — of its analogues

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the end you dipped
reading.explain: This is backwards from a pregnancy test, and it is the single most misread part of drug checking. The strip works by competition: fentanyl in the sample blocks the test line from forming. The drug being present makes a line disappear.
reading.faintLine: A second line can be very faint and still count as negative. A faint line may also appear and then fade — wait the full three minutes before deciding.

procedure: Dissolve the drug in water. How much water depends on the drug and the brand of strip — see below.
Dip the wavy end (not the colored handle) into the solution — commonly about 15 seconds, but check your brand. Do not go past the dotted line.
Lay the strip flat on a dry surface.
Read at the time your instructions give — commonly 3 minutes. Do not read after 10 minutes; a strip left too long can change.

dilution.why: These strips were designed for urine. In water, some substances react with the antibody at high concentration and produce a FALSE POSITIVE. That is the only reason you are told to use more water for methamphetamine and MDMA — they cross-react. Cocaine and heroin do not, so they tolerate a stronger solution.

crossReact.threshold: no false positives found at tested concentrations

dilution.conflict: Published protocols disagree by as much as ten times — CDC, DanceSafe's website, DanceSafe's own printed brochure, and state health departments all give different water volumes. This is not sloppiness: the requirement genuinely differs by strip brand. BTNX 1.0 strips cross-react with meth and MDMA; DanceSafe/WHPM strips were found not to at the same concentration.
guidance: Follow the instructions that came with YOUR strips. Brands differ.
If you do not have them, use MORE water rather than less. Too little water causes false positives on stimulants; only extreme over-dilution risks a false negative.
If a stimulant tests positive, retest with about ten times more water before you act on it. In one street-sample study this corrected every false positive.

commonAmounts.amount: About 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of water per 10 mg
Crush the whole tablet into about 4 tablespoons. Undissolved binder is normal.
A small corner, soaked in 1 teaspoon for 10 minutes

commonAmounts.form: Residue in a cap, cooker or bag
commonAmounts.amount: About 1 mL of clean water onto the residue, after preparing a shot and before drawing it up

dilution.recovery: Testing does not destroy the drug — the water can be evaporated off afterwards.

limits.title: It does not mix evenly
limits.body: Fentanyl mixed into another drug is not distributed evenly. One side of a bag can hold none and the other enough to stop someone breathing. The strongest protection is to dissolve everything you intend to take, test that solution, and then take it. Second best: crush the whole batch to a fine powder and mix it thoroughly before taking a test portion.
limits.nuance: That study looked at batches where fentanyl was the main drug. Hot spots are a bigger risk when fentanyl is a contaminant in something else, and in pressed pills.

limits.title: It misses some analogues
limits.body: In a study of 251 synthetic opioids, 13 compounds were missed by both major brands. Each brand has its own blind spots — roughly 52 for DanceSafe/WHPM strips and 28 for BTNX, in different chemical directions.
limits.nuance: Carfentanil is genuinely disputed. One study found strips failed to detect it below very high concentrations; another found it detected across all lots; a third detected it in real street samples. Treat carfentanil detection as unreliable rather than assured.

limits.title: It does not detect nitazenes at all
limits.body: No fentanyl test strip detects nitazenes. All three nitazenes tested were missed by both brands. A negative fentanyl strip does not rule out a synthetic opioid.

limits.title: Sensitivity varies between batches
limits.body: Labels claim 10–20 ng/mL. Independent testing has found real thresholds as poor as 200 ng/mL. One study found 2017 lots hit 20 ng/mL, while 2021 lots of the same product only reached 200 ng/mL.

limits.title: The strip you buy today may be weaker than the one a study tested
limits.body: Comparing BTNX lots, 2017 strips detected fentanyl at 20 ng/mL while 2021 lots needed 200 ng/mL — a tenfold loss of sensitivity. Cross-reactivity moved the same way: false positives from diphenhydramine started at 100 mg/mL in the old lots and as low as 0.5 mg/mL in the new ones.
limits.nuance: So an accuracy number from a 2018 paper may not describe the strip in your hand in 2026. It is also why diluting properly matters more than which brand you buy.

sources.name: Halifax et al. 2024 — five BTNX lots

strips.accuracy: It was tested against 210 forensic samples. It missed 3.7% of the positives and called 9.6% positive when they were not. That is about 96% sensitivity and 90% specificity, down to 100 ng/mL.

strips.name: Xylazine test strips
strips.detects: Xylazine ("tranq"), a veterinary sedative found in the fentanyl supply — heavily in some regions, rarely in others

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end
reading.explain: Same competitive format as fentanyl strips — one line means detected.

procedure: About 10 mg of drug — a match head, or a grain of rice — in 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of water. Mix well.
Wait 5 minutes — longer than a fentanyl strip.

limits.title: A negative result means much less here
limits.body: In a study of 333 fentanyl-positive street samples, xylazine strips caught only 49% of the samples that actually contained xylazine — 34 of 69. Most samples held less than 1% xylazine by weight, which is below what the strip can see. Roughly half of xylazine-positive samples read negative.

limits.title: False positives on older strips
limits.body: Version 1.0 strips cross-react with lidocaine, methamphetamine, ketamine, and diphenhydramine. The manufacturer says version 2.0 removed the lidocaine cross-reactivity, which matters because lidocaine is a standard cocaine cut. Independent evaluation of those claims is still pending — treat them as manufacturer statements, not verified fact.

limits.title: Naloxone does not reverse xylazine
limits.body: Xylazine is not an opioid. Naloxone will not reverse it — but almost all xylazine in the supply arrives alongside fentanyl, so you should still give naloxone. Watch breathing: if breathing improves, the naloxone worked, even if the person stays sedated.

sources.name: NYC Health — xylazine strip instructions
Community drug checking study, Los Angeles

strips.accuracy: A 2022 evaluation got 20 of 20 xylazine-positive samples right — but on strips that were not commercially available. Across seven brands you can actually buy, detection limits vary by more than double, with BTNX among the weaker ones. Levamisole, a common cocaine adulterant, causes false positives from 0.5 mg/mL.

strips.name: Benzodiazepine test strips
strips.detects: Benzodiazepines as a class — not which one

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end

limits.title: Etizolam is the major gap
limits.body: Etizolam has a different ring structure that the antibody does not bind well, and it is one of the most common benzodiazepines found in the unregulated supply. Validation work reports high sensitivity only when etizolam samples are excluded from the count.

limits.title: Bromazolam IS detected
limits.body: Bromazolam — currently the most prevalent novel benzodiazepine in several unregulated supplies — is detected, because it shares the chemical core the antibody targets.

limits.title: Each new benzodiazepine is a coin flip
limits.body: Detection depends on chemical structure. A newly emerging benzodiazepine may or may not be caught, and there is no way to know until someone tests it specifically.

limits.title: A negative result can itself be informative
limits.body: If a pill sold as pharmaceutical alprazolam tests negative for benzodiazepines, that is a strong sign it is counterfeit.

sources.name: Benzodiazepine strip validation (2025)
Substance Drug Checking — benzodiazepine strips

strips.accuracy: On community drug-checking samples, benzodiazepine strips reached 98% sensitivity and 83% specificity — but only after etizolam-positive samples were removed from the analysis. A positive result was right about 56% of the time; a negative was right about 99% of the time.

strips.name: Nitazene test strips
strips.detects: Some nitazenes — a family of synthetic opioids that fentanyl strips miss entirely

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end

limits.title: Nearly a third of real positives were missed
limits.body: In the only real-world evaluation, BTNX strips missed 29% of nitazene-positive street samples, and caffeine at 11–34% of a sample produced false positives. Readers also reported a very faint negative line on samples both with and without nitazenes, making results hard to call.
limits.nuance: Use them where nitazenes are circulating — a positive is real information. Do not treat a negative as clearance, and check the brand: performance between brands is not comparable.

sources.name: Ontario Drug Checking Community 2026 — 100 street samples

limits.title: Far less sensitive than fentanyl strips
limits.body: Cutoffs run 10 to 100 times higher than a fentanyl strip. One widely sold strip has a 2000 ng/mL cutoff against 10–20 ng/mL for fentanyl strips.

limits.title: Structural blind spots
limits.body: In lab evaluation, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues cross-reacted and 9 were undetectable. Analogues missing a particular chemical group are not detected at all.

limits.title: Still worth using if nitazenes are in your area
limits.body: Nitazene-involved overdose deaths in the US rose from 27 in 2020 to 409 in 2024. Naloxone does work on nitazenes, though multiple doses may be needed.

sources.name: Lab evaluation of nitazene strips

strips.accuracy: Lab results looked strong; real street samples did not. Against 100 samples checked by mass spectrometry, BTNX nitazene strips were 71% sensitive and 76% specific — a 29% false-negative rate. One other brand (Trimedic) was 11% sensitive, missing 89% of positives; that product does not work.

reagentIntro.cannotDetectFentanyl: Fentanyl works in amounts far too small for a reagent to see. Reagents react to the majority substance, not trace substances. Lab testing is what determines exactly what a substance is: FTIR for the bulk, GC-MS for traces like fentanyl.
masking: Not every drug reacts with every reagent
A darker color hides a lighter one
A very small amount of something may produce no visible change at all
reagentIntro.mixtures: Genuine mixtures blend like mixing two colors of paint. If you can see visually different crystals, separate them and test each one.

pureSampleNote.q: Does pure fentanyl react with a reagent?
pureSampleNote.a: In a forensic lab, yes — reference-grade fentanyl does produce a color change. It is irrelevant to anyone holding a bag. Drug checking in Los Angeles found consumer fentanyl averaged 10% fentanyl by weight, pills averaged 1.4%, and 42.5% of samples sold as fentanyl were under 5%. What you have is mostly filler, which is exactly the case reagents cannot read.
pureSampleNote.b: DanceSafe went through a public lab database. Oxycodone with fentanyl in it gave the same reagent colors as clean oxycodone. The pills that came back from overdose deaths looked correct.

reagents.name: Marquis
reagents.useFor: The broad first test. Start here.

reactions.color: Black, often purple or brown tinted
Gray to black — but DELAYED 15–30 seconds, often smoking
reactions.note: The timing, not the final color, is what separates DXM from MDMA

reactions.color: Disputed — no reaction, or light pink to deep peach
reactions.note: Bright orange or red here may mean an amphetamine is present instead

caveats: Cocaine is disputed. Older forensic sources say no reaction; DanceSafe updated in 2023 to expect anything from no reaction to a deep peach or light pink. Bright orange or red on cocaine may mean an amphetamine is present.

reagents.name: Mecke
reagents.base: Selenous acid in concentrated sulfuric acid
caveats: DanceSafe marks Mecke as unvalidated for MDMA/MDA even though it is widely sold as an MDMA reagent.

reagents.name: Simon's
reagents.base: Two-part: sodium nitroprusside with acetaldehyde, then sodium carbonate. Aqueous and alkaline, not an acid.
reagents.useFor: The only common reagent that separates MDMA from MDA, and methamphetamine from amphetamine. Always a second test, never a first.
caveats: The textbook rule that MDA gives no reaction is no longer reliable. Since about 2021 MDA-like substances may produce a muddy gray-green. Both outcomes are now expected, and older charts still teach the old rule.
Listed as inconsistent for 2C-B — do not use it to characterize 2C-x compounds.

reagents.name: Mandelin
reagents.base: Ammonium metavanadate in concentrated sulfuric acid
caveats: Sources disagree on whether to carry it at all. One vendor discontinued it for short shelf life and false positives; another still recommends it for PMA/PMMA screening. DanceSafe marks it unvalidated for MDMA/MDA.
It starts light orange and turns cloudy yellow after 3–4 weeks. That is normal — shake before use.

reagents.name: Froehde
reagents.base: Molybdic acid in hot concentrated sulfuric acid
reagents.useFor: Confirmatory third data point; strong on opioids and MDMA
caveats: Sources conflict on amphetamines: one sequences Froehde as a step for meth/amphetamine, another states no color change. Do not rely on a specific Froehde-amphetamine color.

reagents.name: Liebermann
reagents.base: Potassium or sodium nitrite in concentrated sulfuric acid
reagents.useFor: Secondary reagent for cocaine and ketamine; responds to levamisole

reactions.color: Light yellow to orange — a range is accepted
Very pale yellow, sometimes nearly invisible

caveats: Liebermann alone cannot separate cocaine from a cathinone — both land in the yellow range.

reagents.name: Ehrlich's
reagents.base: p-DMAB in ethanol with concentrated hydrochloric acid
reagents.useFor: The indole reagent, and the single most important LSD test. Use only for LSD and DMT.

reactions.color: Positive, via tryptophan — a genuine false-positive trap

caveats: A negative result on blotter does not mean nothing is there. It fits an NBOMe just as well. That is the thing most often sold as LSD, and it is far more dangerous.
Slow reagent — can take up to 5 minutes, and stays readable for up to an hour.
Ehrlich's does turn purple for psilocybin. It also turns purple for indoles in general, including supermarket mushrooms and death cap. So it cannot tell you a species.

reagents.name: Morris
reagents.useFor: The ketamine and cocaine reagent — the only common reagent giving a strong distinctive ketamine result

reactions.note: Know this color — too small a sample lets the green tint muddy a real result

caveats: Not very sensitive: detection limits are around 1.25 mg.
A "not ketamine" result does not identify what it actually is. Several newer dissociatives are uncharacterized.

procedure.title: Use a pinhead of sample
procedure.body: Finely crushed. Blotter: a tiny corner. Liquids: one drop. Morris: double. For low-dose pressed pills use MORE — a 150 mg pill may hold only 10 mg of active drug.

procedure.title: Never test the whole pill, and never in the bag
procedure.body: Use a white, clean, dry, non-porous surface — ceramic or hard plastic. These reagents are concentrated acids and will destroy a plastic bag. Testing the whole pill destroys the dose and gives an unreadable smear. Pill and blotter dyes distort colors: orange pills throw orange specks, blue pills read muddy brown, and blotter dye is easily mistaken for a purple Ehrlich's positive.

procedure.title: One drop, and never touch the sample with the bottle
procedure.body: Touching the tip to the sample contaminates the entire bottle. Hold the cap upside down while you work — setting it down, or on the wrong bottle, is a common mistake. For two-part reagents, both drops go on the SAME sample.

procedure.title: Watch from the moment the drop lands
procedure.body: Intermediate colors carry information — that is how Marquis separates MDMA from DXM. Read within roughly the first minute and disregard later drift from air and moisture. Sources give anywhere from 40 seconds to 3 minutes, so there is no single correct number. Ehrlich's, Hofmann, and Morris are the slow exceptions at about 5 minutes.

procedure.title: Use several reagents, with a fresh sample each time
procedure.body: Never drop a second reagent onto an already-tested spot. Re-cap before opening the next bottle. One reagent narrows it down; several together tell you much more, because each one rules out something different.

procedure.title: Run a blank next to it
procedure.body: Put a drop of the reagent alone beside your test spot. Reagents are tinted and darken with age, so a blank tells you what "no reaction" looks like today. Use neutral daylight. If unsure, retest with a larger sample.

procedure.title: Clean up
procedure.body: Neutralize with baking soda, wash with soap and water, and dry before the next test.

safety.ppe: Wear gloves and eye protection. Marquis, Mecke, Mandelin, Froehde, Liebermann and Hofmann are concentrated sulfuric acid; Ehrlich's is hydrochloric acid in ethanol. They damage skin and eyes. Work in a ventilated area — DXM on Marquis often smokes.
firstAid: Eyes: flood with water for at least 10 minutes, holding the eye open.
Swallowed: rinse the mouth, do NOT induce vomiting, drink water, get medical help immediately.
safety.storage: Keep upright, lid secured, away from heat and light. Refrigerated they last 1–2 years; at room temperature that roughly halves. Let them warm up before opening, since condensation and cold change how they react.
safety.expiry: Marquis and Mecke darken as they age. A reagent is expired when it is too dark to read a reaction clearly. Dark green or black means contamination — discard it.
safety.validate: Test a drop on sugar. If you cannot see a clear reaction, the reagent may no longer be accurate.
safety.disposal: Neutralize the spent drop with baking soda and rinse the surface with plenty of water. Take unused or expired reagent to a household hazardous waste facility. Never pour concentrated acid neat down a drain, and never mix reagents together.

legal.headline: Test strips are legal in most, but not all, states
legal.body: The same carve-out covers xylazine strips in 36 states plus DC. Ohio and Florida joined after the earlier count. Reagent kits are covered in fewer states still. So a strip that is legal for one drug may not be legal for another.
legal.stale: Lists circulating online are out of date. Idaho changed in July 2024 and Indiana in 2025, so the commonly repeated five-state list is wrong. As of July 2026 the three remaining states where possessing drug-checking equipment may still be criminal are Iowa, North Dakota and Texas.
legal.advice: Check your own state's current law. Nothing here is legal advice.

labs.intro: Only a laboratory can confirm what is actually in a sample. Most of these take samples through a harm reduction program rather than from individuals — check each one before you post anything.
labs.note: DrugsData.org paused accepting new samples in April 2024 and does not expect to resume before 2027. Its historical archive is still worth searching, but do not mail samples there.

options.name: UNC Street Drug Analysis Lab
options.detail: GC-MS, nationwide US — submitted through a harm reduction program, not by individuals. Free kits for US harm reduction organizations, and free in North Carolina and for drug user unions.

options.name: Transparency Testing
options.detail: Mail-in FTIR, LC-MS and NMR; quantitative

options.name: WEDINOS
options.detail: Free anonymous postal testing (Public Health Wales); does not report purity or dose

options.name: Find a service near you
options.detail: Most in-person drug checking runs through syringe service programs

how.title: What a lab does that a strip cannot
how.intro: A strip answers one yes/no question about one substance. These identify everything in a sample, and some of them say how much.

methods.name: FTIR — infrared spectroscopy
methods.what: Shines infrared light through the sample and reads which wavelengths it absorbs. Every compound has a distinct absorption pattern, so the machine matches that pattern against a library.
methods.good: Seconds to run, no sample destroyed, and it is what most in-person drug checking services actually use — you can often watch it happen and ask questions.
methods.limits: It reads the BULK of a sample. Anything under roughly 5% by weight can be invisible to it, which means it routinely misses fentanyl at street concentrations. That is why services run FTIR and a fentanyl strip together, not one instead of the other.

methods.name: GC-MS — gas chromatography–mass spectrometry
methods.what: Separates a mixture into its individual components, then weighs each one's molecular fragments to identify it. The chromatography does the separating; the mass spectrometry does the identifying.
methods.good: The reference standard. It finds trace components an FTIR cannot see, including fentanyl analogues and adulterants present in tiny amounts, and it names them specifically rather than by family.
methods.limits: Needs a laboratory, trained staff, and days rather than seconds. This is what mail-in programs use, and the wait is the trade-off for the detail.

methods.name: LC-MS and NMR
methods.what: Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry handles compounds that GC cannot vaporize. NMR reads how atomic nuclei behave in a magnetic field and can determine structure and quantity.
methods.good: Together these give quantitative answers — not just what is present, but how much. That is the only way to know a percentage rather than a yes.
methods.limits: The most expensive and least available. Only a handful of programs offer it.

how.bottom: Nothing here is instant, and none of it tells you about the batch you did not send. What a lab result changes is what you know about your supply in general — and, through published results, what everyone else in your area knows too.

companion: A smaller amount first, with time before any more, is what tells you about a batch before it tells you the hard way. It matters most with something new, or after any time away — tolerance drops faster than people expect.

Using alone is what turns most overdoses into accidents — not the dose, the fact that nobody was there to notice. If there is no one around, Never Use Alone answers 24/7 at 1-800-484-3731 and sends help if you stop responding.
Carry naloxone, and make sure whoever is with you knows where it is.
Fentanyl and nitazenes are opioids — naloxone works on both. It may take more than one dose.

storage.headline: Storing your supplies
storage.intro: Every one of these degrades, and a degraded test does not announce itself — it just gives you a wrong answer in the same confident colors.

items.how: Fridge if you can, dark and cool if you cannot. Keep them in the box they came in.
items.why: Light and heat break them down. Reagents darken with age — a Marquis that has gone brown on its own will read as a reaction that never happened. This is why running a blank drop beside your test matters: it shows you what the bottle looks like today.
items.life: Roughly a year refrigerated, much less if warm. Replace them if the color has drifted.

items.how: Room temperature, sealed in their pouch until the moment you use one. Not the glovebox, not the bathroom.
items.why: Humidity is the enemy — the pouch is sealed for a reason, and a strip that has taken on moisture can fail in either direction. Heat cycling in a car does the same.
items.life: Check the printed expiry. An expired strip is not a maybe.

items.how: Room temperature, out of direct light, somewhere you can reach it in the dark and someone else can find it.
items.why: It tolerates ordinary conditions well but not extremes. A car in summer or a freezing porch is genuinely too much. Nasal spray works fine after freezing IF it has fully thawed — but if you only have one dose, do not rely on that.
items.life: Expiry dates are conservative. Expired naloxone loses potency over time but is far better than none — if it is what you have, use it and call 911.

items.how: Somewhere another person can find it without you telling them where.
items.why: Naloxone in a locked box in your room helps nobody if you are the one who is not breathing. Whoever is around needs to know it exists and be able to reach it.

sources.name: DanceSafe — reagent testing kit instructions
FDA — naloxone nasal spray label (storage section)

compare.headline: Which test tells you what
compare.intro: No single tool answers every question, and the differences between them are not small. This is the short version; each tool has its own section below with the detail and the sources.
compare.note: Every one of these is better at saying yes than at saying no. They also do better in a lab than on real street samples. The numbers here are the street ones.

rows.finds: Fentanyl and many of its analogues
rows.misses: Nitazenes entirely. Some analogues. Uneven mixing in a bag.
rows.negative: Fairly strong — about 96% sensitivity against 210 forensic samples. But sensitivity varies tenfold between manufacturing lots, so dilute properly.

rows.misses: Medetomidine, which is now replacing xylazine in some places and does not cross-react.
rows.negative: Weak. A negative rules out xylazine, not sedation — medetomidine does not cross-react. Levamisole causes false positives.

rows.finds: Benzodiazepines as a class — never which one
rows.misses: Etizolam, the major gap. Each newly appearing benzo is a coin flip.
rows.negative: Moderate. 98% sensitive only once etizolam samples are excluded; a positive is right about 56% of the time.

rows.finds: Some nitazenes — the family fentanyl strips miss
rows.misses: Structural blind spots; far less sensitive than fentanyl strips.
rows.negative: Weak — 29% of real positives were missed in the only street-sample study, and one brand missed 89%. A positive means something; a negative does not.

rows.finds: What the BULK of a sample mostly is
rows.misses: Anything present in small amounts — including fentanyl at street concentrations. Colors can mask each other in a mixture.
rows.negative: Different question entirely. Reagents identify the main substance; they do not screen for contaminants.

rows.misses: Nothing technical — the limit is time and access.
rows.negative: Strongest available. The trade-off is days of turnaround and, for most people, going through a local program.

buying.headline: Buying it over the counter
buying.intro: The same shelf carries a product that looks almost the same and answers a completely different question. So it is worth knowing exactly what to pick up.

trap.title: Most “fentanyl test strips” sold in stores test a person, not a drug
trap.body: A urine drug screen tells you whether someone has already taken something. It cannot tell you what is in a bag. Both are strips in a pouch, both are immunoassays, and they sit in the same aisle under nearly the same words.
trap.tell: How to tell them apart: a substance-checking kit comes with a micro-scoop and a small measuring cup, because you dissolve a sample in water. A urine screen mentions urine, a dip card or cassette, a panel count, or “CLIA waived”. If it costs more and includes a mail-in lab envelope, it is a urine screen.
trap.examples: Verified in August 2026: Walmart’s entire “fentanyl strips” category — all 23 results — was urine screens. CVS sells both, with the urine kit at roughly twice the price of the real thing, and its own listing text mixed up which drug it tests for.

items.price: About $35 for a two-dose Narcan carton at CVS
items.note: Over the counter since 2023, with a third brand approved in June 2026. Free is often possible — see Learn for programs that mail it after a short course.

items.where: CVS, in stores and online, in 37 states
items.price: About $10 for 10 strips with scoops and a cup
items.note: Look for “DrugCheck” or any pack that includes micro-scoops. Cheaper per strip from DanceSafe or Amazon (roughly $1.50–$2 each). CVS’s own listing notes it is restricted in some states.

items.where: Not on any pharmacy shelf we could confirm — online, or free from a harm reduction program
items.price: Xylazine strips $1.69 each from Grassroots Harm Reduction, $1.99 from DanceSafe — or free from a local program
items.note: Benzodiazepine strips are not sold by DanceSafe; Grassroots and local programs are the routes. Nitazene strips run about $3.

items.where: Online — DanceSafe, Bunk Police — or free through some harm reduction programs
items.price: About $20 for a single-reagent kit, $89–119 for a set; sometimes free through a program
items.note: No retail chain sells these. A local program may have kits on hand or test with you.

items.what: Free, from a harm reduction program
items.where: Local programs and peer-run networks — no purchase at all
items.note: Programs stock up through Grassroots Harm Reduction. It is a buyers' club, open to any group that gives supplies away free. If you run a program, or want to start one, that is where the supply comes from.

legal.title: Whether you can buy them depends on your state
legal.body: Drug-checking equipment is fully legal to sell, give away and possess in 20 states. Thirteen more allow it only for specific drugs — usually fentanyl strips. In Iowa, North Dakota and Texas, possessing it arguably remains a crime. Puerto Rico's status is unknown rather than clear — the July 2026 review covers four of five territories without naming which ones. Massachusetts and Michigan allow possession and free distribution but not sale.
legal.note: These laws are actively changing. The counts above are from a July 2026 review; anything you read elsewhere without a date on it is probably older. Availability varies by store and by state and cannot be verified nationally — if a chain near you does not carry it, a local harm reduction program can.

storefronts.title: Where to buy from a legitimate source
storefronts.intro: These sellers are worth trusting. They are harm reduction groups that publish what their products do and do not detect. On a marketplace, the accuracy claims are written by whoever is selling.

shops.name: Grassroots Harm Reduction
shops.carries: Fentanyl strips $1.49 · xylazine strips $1.69 · reagents · purity kits · drug info cards
shops.why: Run by DanceSafe’s founder, and the cheapest per-strip source we found. All proceeds are redistributed to independent peer-run harm reduction groups. Organizations can register for buyers’ club pricing; anyone can buy at the listed price.

shops.name: DanceSafe
shops.carries: Fentanyl strips $1.99 · xylazine $1.99 · nitazene $3.00 · reagent kits from $20
shops.why: The original nonprofit in this space. Their instructions state plainly what reagents cannot tell you, which is rarer than it should be.

shops.name: Bunk Police
shops.why: Long-running reagent supplier; kits come with substance-specific color charts.

shops.name: NEXT Distro
shops.carries: Naloxone and fentanyl strips, by mail
shops.why: Free rather than for sale, where your state allows it. Usually requires a short online training first.

avoid.title: What to be careful of on a marketplace
avoid.body: Amazon and similar carry real strips alongside listings advertising “99% accurate” with no study behind the number, and urine screens named to look like drug-checking strips. If a listing will not tell you which analogues it misses, it is selling confidence rather than information.

brands.headline: Which strip do you have?
brands.intro: Two fentanyl strips are in wide use. One wants five times more water than the other. They are read two minutes apart. And they do not find the same things.

notInterchangeable.title: The two fentanyl brands miss different drugs
notInterchangeable.body: That is not a reason to distrust the one you have. It is the reason a negative result is weaker than a positive one. It is also why programs hand out both when they can.

source.name: Assessment of two brands of fentanyl test strips with 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

items.name: BTNX Rapid Response
items.maker: Made by BTNX. Commonly what a syringe service program or health department hands out.
items.sample: 10 mg of drug — about a match head or a grain of rice — crushed and mixed.
items.water: 5 mL of water for every 10 mg — one teaspoon. If you cook a shot, that is a full cooker.
items.residue: Testing residue instead? That is what is left in a cap, a cooker, or the corner of a bag. Add 2 mL of clean water, about half a teaspoon, and mix well.
items.dip: Dip for 15 seconds, holding the dark blue end.
items.dipLimit: Do not dip past the wavy blue lines.
items.negative: TWO red lines — look closely, the second can be very faint
items.invalid: A line only on the left, or no lines at all. Redo it with a new strip.
items.blindSpot: It missed 52 of the fentanyl analogues in the lab screen. That is more misses than the other brand. It did find more compounds overall at high amounts: 173 against 149.

sources.name: Washington State DOH — Using BTNX Rapid Response Fentanyl Test Strips (DOH 150-240)
Assessment of two brands of fentanyl test strips with 251 synthetic opioids (Harm Reduct J, 2023)

opioid.label: Heroin, fentanyl or another opioid
opioid.note: The standard amount above. Opioids do not cross-react with this strip.

cocaine.label: Cocaine
cocaine.note: The standard amount above — do not over-dilute it. Cocaine was tested and produced no false positives at any concentration tried, so it does not need the stimulant treatment. Lidocaine, a common cocaine cut, does fool the strip from about 2.5 mg per mL, which the standard amount already sits under.

sources.name: High concentrations of illicit stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl test strips (Harm Reduct J, 2021)

stim.label: Meth or MDMA
stim.water: 10 mg into 20 mL — four teaspoons. Four times the usual amount.
stim.note: The usual 5 mL puts the sample at 2 mg per mL. At that strength this strip reads positive with no fentanyl in it at all: 1.5 mg/mL of methamphetamine, or 2 mg/mL of MDMA, is enough to do it.

sources.name: High concentrations of illicit stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl test strips (Harm Reduct J, 2021)

ketamine.label: Ketamine
ketamine.note: Ketamine was not in the cross-reaction study, so there is no published number either way. Dilute anyway: ketamine is usually taken with something else, and that something else is what the list is about.

sources.name: High concentrations of illicit stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl test strips (Harm Reduct J, 2021)

unknown.label: An unknown powder
unknown.note: Diphenhydramine — Benadryl — fools this strip from 1 mg per mL. That is lower than meth or MDMA. It is also a common cut in powders sold as anything.

sources.name: High concentrations of illicit stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl test strips (Harm Reduct J, 2021)

pill.label: A pill, pressed or pharmaceutical
pill.note: Crush it completely first, then use the standard amount. A pill dropped in whole only wets its surface, and fentanyl is not spread evenly through a pressed tablet — one corner can carry all of it.

blotter.label: Blotter or a tab
blotter.water: Soak it in 5 mL — one teaspoon — for about 10 minutes.
blotter.note: It has to actually come off the paper, which takes longer than a dip.

residue.label: Residue in a cap, cooker or bag
residue.water: 2 mL of clean water — about half a teaspoon.
residue.note: Nothing to weigh: the residue is the sample. Rinse it around and test the rinse.

items.name: DanceSafe
items.maker: Since 12 March 2026 the store and the shipping are run by Transparency, the group behind Bunk Police. The strip and its instructions did not change. The packet may just arrive with a different name on it.
items.sample: 10 mg of drug — about a match head or a grain of rice — crushed and mixed.
items.water: 1 mL of water for every 10 mg — about 20 drops, or a fifth of a teaspoon.
items.residue: Testing residue instead? That is what is left in a cap, a cooker, or the corner of a bag. Add 2 mL of clean water, about half a teaspoon, and mix well.
items.dip: Dip for 15 seconds, holding the yellow end.
items.dipLimit: Do not dip past the dotted area.
items.wait: Wait 3 minutes, with the strip face up on a flat surface.
items.negative: TWO red lines — look closely, the second can be very faint
items.invalid: A line only on the left, or no lines at all. Redo it with a new strip.
items.blindSpot: It missed 28 of the fentanyl analogues in the lab screen. But it was the better of the two at low amounts: at 200 ng/mL it found almost 2.5 times as many.

brands.gap: Wondfo, DetectaChem, Lochness Medical and MD-Bio are not here yet. Neither are benzodiazepine or nitazene strips. We only print a number once we have read it off the sheet it came from.
brands.notListed: Not listed? Most strips sold for harm reduction in the US are made by one of two companies — BTNX or WHPM — whatever name is on the front. DanceSafe, Bunk Police and Grassroots all sell the same WHPM strip. Look for the maker on the packet, the box or the insert and use that row. If it names neither, your insert is the authority.
brands.lotsTitle: Read the instructions that came with your strips
brands.lots: Strips are not interchangeable, and a brand can change between lots. Dip time, how long a result stays valid and how much water to use have all differed between batches from the same maker. The row above is that product's published procedure; the paper in your packet is that packet's.
